title: Model-sized tools/call write to a stalled --local-mcp server blocks the main thread with no deadline, and Ctrl-C/SIGTERM/SIGHUP cannot interrupt it
description: LocalMcp::send writes each JSON-RPC line to the --local-mcp server's stdin with a blocking ChildStdin::write_all and flush on the main thread. The only deadline (ASK_CLAUDE_LOCAL_MCP_TIMEOUT, default 120 s) and the only interrupt checks cover the read side and the moment before a send. When a tools/call times out (Unanswered::Late), the server may still be busy and not reading stdin. The untrusted model can then issue another custom tool call that the gate allows, in the same round or a later one (at most ROUNDS=8 custom rounds per turn). If the tools/call line, alone or added to earlier unread lines, exceeds the free pipe capacity (64 KiB by default on Linux, less under pipe-user-pages limits), write(2) blocks until the server reads again. The SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers only set INTERRUPTED and use SA_RESTART. Even without SA_RESTART, Rust's write_all retries on EINTR. So the write never returns to a point where interrupted() is checked, and the KTD11 path (exit 130, user.interrupt POST, server stop) waits until the write completes. The server runs in its own process group, so terminal Ctrl-C does not reach it. The CLI recovers on its own if the server finishes its busy call and drains stdin. It also recovers if the user kills the server's process group: the write then fails with EPIPE (SIGPIPE is ignored for the write), send returns false, the remaining calls see the flag, and the interrupt path runs. If the server never drains, the user's remaining exits are SIGQUIT or SIGKILL of ask-claude, which skip Drop/stop, leave the server group running and post no user.interrupt. The bash oracle writes through a `cat >&7` child in the foreground process group, so terminal Ctrl-C kills that child and the INT path continues. A SIGTERM aimed only at the bash script's pid would also wait for the foreground child, so the contrast holds for terminal-delivered signals only. Shown from source, the impact is limited to the user's own CLI: loss of the graceful stop control and an orphaned server group on a hard kill. Any shared or operator-owned effect depends on unverified provider behavior.
claimed_root_cause: LocalMcp::send (rust/src/local_mcp.rs:169-188) does a blocking ChildStdin::write_all/flush on the main thread, with no deadline, writer thread, non-blocking mode or interrupt check during the write. LocalTools::call checks interrupted() only once, before the send (local_mcp.rs:304). catch_signals (rust/src/transport.rs:272-284) installs SA_RESTART handlers that only store INTERRUPTED. A pipe write(2) blocked with nothing written is restarted, and std's write_all retries any EINTR in any case, so the flag is not read until the server drains the pipe or closes it. Removing SA_RESTART alone would not fix this. The send needs its own deadline or interruptible wait.

trace.description: A requires_action fold carrying custom tool uses from the untrusted model is answered on the main thread through self.answer, for up to ROUNDS=8 custom rounds per turn (agent.rs:25, 806-809).

Each custom tool use that the server lists (has) and the gate allows (ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM=allow, a tty yes, or an in-memory 'always' for the shown name) goes to LocalTools::call, one after another. The gate does not cap the input size.
An earlier call whose read passes the timeout returns an error result (Late), while the server may still be busy and not reading stdin.
The next call copies the model-controlled input verbatim into params.arguments with no size cap and sends it (308). The only interrupted() check is at 304, before the send.
A blocking write_all/flush to the server's stdin pipe with no deadline. It blocks once the unread bytes exceed the free pipe capacity, and signals do not break it out.

evidence.description: `let sent = stdin.write_all(&line).and_then(|()| stdin.flush());` is a blocking write on an unbuffered ChildStdin with no timeout or interrupt check. send() returns false only on an error such as EPIPE.
Only read() has a deadline: recv_timeout bounded by the timeout and TICK, with interrupted() checked at 199. Nothing equivalent guards send().
call() checks interrupted() once, before the send. A signal that arrives during a blocked write is first seen in read() (199) after the write completes.

`action.sa_flags = libc::SA_RESTART;` applies to SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP (280-281). on_signal only stores INTERRUPTED (265), so a pipe write blocked with nothing written is restarted. std's write_all also retries ErrorKind::Interrupted.
process_group(0) puts the server in its own process group, so a terminal SIGINT/SIGHUP does not reach the peer that must drain the pipe.
stop() runs only from Drop. It is unreachable while the main thread is blocked in send(), and it is skipped after SIGKILL/SIGQUIT, which leaves the server group running.
Oracle contrast: the bash twin writes through a `cat >&7` subshell child in the foreground process group, which a terminal Ctrl-C kills, so the send fails and INT handling continues.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox is available in this run (no network isolation, no empty allowlisted environment, no read-only target with scratch-only writes, no resource or time limits), so no fixture or built binary may be executed. That a full pipe blocks the restarted write and that SIGINT does not end it has not been observed locally. It follows from source, from Linux pipe semantics and from std write_all's EINTR retry.

Whether real stdio MCP servers stop draining stdin while a tools/call runs, and long enough to pass the timeout (default 120 s), is outside the repository. Servers built on async SDKs usually keep reading, while sequential read-process-write servers do not. The hang lasts forever only if the busy call never finishes. The trigger also needs a model-sized argument, or unread lines from earlier timed-out calls, larger than the free pipe capacity (64 KiB by default on Linux).

Whether a Managed Agents session left in requires_action with an unanswered custom tool use and no user.interrupt keeps charging operator-owned spend or holds a container is a provider fact outside the repository. Without it, the source-visible impact is confined to the user's own process: the graceful Ctrl-C/SIGTERM/SIGHUP stop is lost, and a hard kill orphans the server group. Under the resource-exhaustion rules that is hardening rather than a shared-impact vulnerability.

Use a --local-mcp fixture shell server that answers initialize and tools/list for one tool named `slow`. On the first tools/call it stops reading stdin and sleeps longer than the test limit, without exiting. Set ASK_CLAUDE_LOCAL_MCP_TIMEOUT=1 and ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM=allow. The replayed stream requests two `slow` custom tool uses in one requires_action round, the second with an `input` string of about 128 KiB. Then, from the harness, kill the fixture's process group and assert that ask-claude exits 130 promptly (the recovery path). Tear down every fixture process when the sandbox ends.

The owner should also confirm whether the stdio MCP servers users run with --local-mcp read stdin concurrently with tools/call execution.

title: Per-host MCP token variable fold is non-injective, so another host can receive a server's token
description: token_variable (rust/src/request.rs:133-138) builds ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_<HOST> from host() (request.rs:107-119), which turns every char outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] into '-', then upper-cases and turns '-' into '_'. '.', '-' and '_' therefore all become '_', so distinct DNS hosts such as mcp.good.example and mcp-good.example (a separately registrable domain) both read ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_MCP_GOOD_EXAMPLE. Every IPv6-literal host also reads ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN__, because url_host (rust/src/lib.rs:693) cuts '[::1]' at the first ':' and leaves '['. A user who keeps the good server's token exported (the documented per-host setup, and the environment is often set for other tools) and runs --mcp https://mcp-good.example/... (a lookalike or a recommended third-party server) gets that token placed in authorization_token on the lookalike's mcp_servers entry (request.rs:57-59). If both hosts are on one command line, both entries carry the same token and the same name/mcp_server_name (request.rs:56,161). config::check refuses the shared ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN with several servers for exactly this reason (config.rs:108-116), but it only uses the per-host names it computes (config.rs:80) in an error message. It never checks them for collisions, and nothing binds a token to one exact host. The bash oracle shares the pattern (lib/request.jq:73), and run 2 locally confirmed it at low severity as lib/request.jq:mcp_token:host-variable-name-collision. That strengthens the Rust finding, since the goldens hold the two to the same bytes. The Rust path was verified from source only.
claimed_root_cause: token_variable (rust/src/request.rs:133-138) is a lossy, non-injective encoding of the host (host() at request.rs:107-119 collapses '.', '-', '_' and any other byte to one character), and neither config::check (rust/src/config.rs:73-116) nor request::body checks that a token variable or server name maps to exactly one distinct host. So the variable does not bind the credential to a single server.

trace.description: --mcp https://mcp-good.example/mcp (alone, or alongside https://mcp.good.example/mcp) as a repeatable global flag. The help text at line 143 promises the token comes from ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_<HOST>. The URL comes from a lower-trust third party (a lookalike or recommended server), and the token was exported for a different host.

Requires only an https:// prefix (line 76) and computes each server's token variable only for the shared-token error message. There is no uniqueness check across servers, and nothing compares an exported per-host variable with the exact host. The only refusal is for the shared ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN with several servers (lines 110-116).
Forwards r.mcp unchanged into request::Args.mcp.

Every char outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] (including '.') becomes '-', so mcp.good.example and mcp-good.example both become mcp-good-example. For https://[::1]/x, url_host (lib.rs:693) yields '[', which becomes '-'.
Upper-cases and maps '-' to '_', giving ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_MCP_GOOD_EXAMPLE for both hosts (and ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN__ for every IPv6 literal).
Reads that variable from the environment and returns its non-empty value for whichever URL produced the name, here the lookalike host's URL.
authorization_token is set on the mcp-good.example mcp_servers entry in the Messages request body. The MCP connector is expected to present it to the server at that URL (not observable from source).

evidence.description: token_variable: format!("ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_{}", host(url).to_ascii_uppercase().replace('-', "_")). The doc comment (129-132) calls it 'the variable this server's own token is read from'.
host(): url_host cut at '/' or ':', with every char outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] mapped to '-' (lines 111-117).
url_host takes the text before the first stop char, so an IPv6 literal '[::1]' is cut to '[' and every IPv6 host folds to the same variable ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN__.

Comment states the invariant: 'a token is one server's credential: sent to several, each server's operator would receive the others''. It is enforced only for the shared ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN (110-116), not for colliding per-host variables.
Colliding hosts also get the same mcp_servers name, and toolset (line 161) the same mcp_server_name, so the two-server variant sends two entries with one ambiguous name and one shared token.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox is available in this run, so no target code (cargo test, or a harness calling request::token_variable/request::body) may be executed. The Rust request body containing the colliding token is established from source only, not locally observed. The bash twin's identical behavior was locally observed in run 2.

That the Messages API MCP connector presents authorization_token as a bearer credential to the server at the entry's URL is provider behavior that is not observable from source or offline. For the two-server variant, whether the API rejects or routes two mcp_servers entries with the same name is also unobservable, and decides whether that variant reaches either server. The single-server lookalike variant does not depend on duplicate-name handling.

A fix should make (2) carry no token and (3) exit 2.

They set only ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_MCP_OWNER_TEST_EXAMPLE=dummy-not-real and run one request with --mcp https://mcp-owner-test.example/mcp, then one with both URLs. They record which endpoint receives 'Authorization: Bearer dummy-not-real', and whether the API returns an error for the duplicate mcp_servers name.

title: Untrusted retrieved content can drive every tool of a credentialed --mcp server with no deterministic gate
description: On the Messages path, request::body puts web_search/web_fetch (with --web, no allowed_domains) and one mcp_toolset per --mcp server into the same tools array, and mcp_servers carries each server's authorization_token (ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_<HOST>, or the shared token for a lone server). toolset emits {type, mcp_server_name} with no default_config unless an --mcp-tool entry names that host, so by default every tool the server lists is enabled. The connector runs these calls on Anthropic's side inside one response, so the client cannot confirm a call; it only prints '(mcp <server>)' (no tool name or input) as the block streams. Reply content, including third-party web_fetch/web_search results and other servers' mcp_tool_result blocks, is appended to the history and resent on each pause_turn continuation (up to 8, no user step) and each chat turn. A third party who controls a fetched page or search result, or the operator of a second --mcp server, can therefore try to make the model call any enabled tool of a token-bearing server (including write or exfiltration tools, with -f contents available in context) under the user's token, an exact action the user did not request. config::check refuses non-https --mcp, unmatched --mcp-tool hosts and a shared token across several servers, but neither refuses nor warns on --web with an un-allowlisted --mcp server or on several servers sharing one context. Since the bash run-2 record (lib/request.jq:tools:mcp-toolset-unconfirmed-with-untrusted-retrieval) the project added the --mcp-tool allowlist and README.md:34-42 now discloses that ask-claude cannot ask before a call and that a server no --mcp-tool names keeps all its tools; the Rust port, held to the bash oracle by goldens, shares this default. The residual is a disclosed default: no deterministic control binds the action to user intent unless the user opts into an allowlist. Whether a model follows injected content to make such a call, and whether the owner treats a bare --mcp as approval of every tool, are not observable from source.
claimed_root_cause: toolset (rust/src/request.rs:152-171) leaves every --mcp server with all tools enabled unless --mcp-tool names its host, and body (rust/src/request.rs:46-89) composes that token-bearing toolset with untrusted retrieval tools (web_search/web_fetch) and other servers' toolsets in one request, while config::check (rust/src/config.rs:53-130) neither narrows nor refuses that composition. Because the connector executes calls API-side within the response, the only possible source-side action binding is the enabled-tool set, and by default it is the server's whole tool list, so the binding of an MCP action to user intent rests on the model alone.

trace.description: Lower-trust entry: the reply's full content array, which carries third-party web_search/web_fetch results and other MCP servers' mcp_tool_result blocks, is appended to the history. Within a single response the third-party content reaches the model API-side before any of it reaches the client, so there is no client hook between injection and call.
A pause_turn reply is continued automatically (up to 8 rounds, no user step) with the same tools; each round rebuilds the body at lib.rs:463.
The history, including the earlier third-party tool results and any -f contents in the first user turn, is resent as messages.
Checks https scheme, --mcp-tool host matching and the shared-token refusal only; no refusal, opt-in or warning for --web with an un-allowlisted --mcp server or several servers in one context.
The server's own token (ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN_<HOST>, or the shared token for a lone server) is attached as authorization_token.
web_search and web_fetch (max_uses 5, no allowed_domains) are added to the same tools array, so third-party content enters the model context.

Boundary effect: mcp_toolset is emitted as {type, mcp_server_name} with no default_config, so every tool of the token-bearing server is callable by the model and executed API-side without client confirmation.

evidence.description: default_config {enabled:false} plus per-tool configs only when an --mcp-tool entry's host matches this server; otherwise all tools stay on.
One toolset per --mcp server pushed after the web tools in the same tools array.
--web flag (user configuration, full trust); --mcp at cli.rs:145 and --mcp-tool at cli.rs:153, whose help text states 'a server not named keeps all its tools'.
The only multi-server control refuses a shared ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN for several servers; per-host tokens for several servers sharing one context pass.
While a call runs the user sees only '(mcp <server>)', never the tool name or its input.

Discloses that Anthropic calls the MCP server from its side so ask-claude cannot ask before a call, that tool inputs (including -f contents) reach the operator, and (README.md:39-40) that a server no --mcp-tool names keeps all its tools: a documented default.

blockers: Model and API behavior not observable from source: whether the model, given attacker-written web_fetch/web_search content or another server's mcp_tool_result, issues an mcp_tool_use to an enabled tool of a token-bearing server that the user did not request.

Owner intent not observable from source: README.md:34-42 and the --mcp-tool help disclose that a bare --mcp keeps every tool and that no per-call confirmation is possible; whether the owner treats that generic opt-in as the intended approval of every tool (an accepted trade-off) or wants a deterministic refusal/opt-in for --web or several servers without an allowlist decides whether this is a defect.

Run ask-claude --web --mcp <owner server> (no --mcp-tool) -f <dummy file> with a prompt asking only to summarize that page; record from ASK_CLAUDE_REQUEST_LOG/event log and the server's log whether an mcp_tool_use for note_write was issued. Separately record the owner's decision on whether a bare --mcp is intended to approve every tool.

title: Rust --memory access suffix other than exact ':ro' silently attaches the memory store without read_only
description: --memory takes <id>[:ro] (rust/src/cli.rs:225-227, README.md:261-262). Agent::new checks only that the text before the first ':' starts with memstore_ and that there are at most 8 entries (rust/src/agent.rs:470-484). session::create_body sets access:read_only only when the second ':'-field is exactly "ro" (rust/src/session.rs:159-166). Every other suffix produces a memory_store resource with no access field, and there is no error branch: ':RO', ':readonly', ':read_only', ':rw' and an empty ':' suffix all do this. A suffix like ':ro:x' still gets read_only. Agent::create passes the same self.memories (cloned from argv at agent.rs:548) to every session the run creates, including sessions started after /new (agent.rs:634-652), and POSTs the body to /sessions (agent.rs:697-700). So a user who asks for read-only with any spelling other than exact ':ro' gets no warning, and the store is attached with the provider's default access. The entrypoint is the trusted local user's own argv. The security-relevant actor is untrusted session content (a mounted repository, fetched web pages, MCP results) that steers the agent. If the provider default is writable, that content can make the agent write durable entries into a store the user meant to keep read-only. Later sessions that attach the store, including other agents or users of the same workspace store, read those entries back as memory. This is the same root cause as the open bash record lib/session-create.jq:memory_resource:unrecognized-access-suffix-fails-open, and the goldens hold the Rust port to the same bytes.
claimed_root_cause: rust/src/session.rs:160-164 maps the access suffix with `if parts.next() == Some("ro") { r["access"] = json!("read_only"); }`, a case-sensitive exact match with no rejection branch. rust/src/agent.rs:471-478 validates only the id prefix (`m.split(':').next()...starts_with("memstore_")`), even though its error text advertises ':ro for read-only'. title: Proxy environment routes the plain-http loopback API request, API key included, through a network proxy
description: base_url_gate accepts plain http only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], 'so the key never travels in clear over a network' (rust/src/config.rs:218-219, check at 234). Both HTTP transports build their ureq agents from ureq::Agent::config_builder() and set http_status_as_error, max_redirects(0) and both timeouts, but never touch the proxy (rust/src/transport.rs:47-52; rust/src/transport/sessions.rs:124-133). No file under rust/src mentions a proxy. ureq is pinned at =3.5.2 (rust/Cargo.toml:31). Its Cargo.lock checksum 3ac5cecf...a59d matches the sha256 of the locally cached .crate. In that crate, Config::default sets proxy: Proxy::try_from_env() (src/config.rs:1073). try_from_env takes the first parseable value among ALL_PROXY, all_proxy, HTTPS_PROXY, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY and http_proxy, whatever the target's scheme (src/proxy.rs:232-249). So a variable a user sets only for https traffic also catches the http loopback request. connect_proxy_uri does not check the scheme (src/config.rs:251-259). For an http or https proxy, the CONNECT connector (src/unversioned/transport/connect.rs:37-56, 109) sends 'CONNECT <target_host>:<port>' unless NO_PROXY matches, and the proxy side resolves the target (src/proxy.rs:56-59, resolve_target=false). The application then writes the HTTP/1.1 request into that tunnel without TLS. The request carries x-api-key (transport.rs:84; sessions.rs:148, 224) or Authorization: Bearer for -p openai (transport.rs:81). Its body can carry mcp_servers[].authorization_token (request.rs:59) or, for agent --repo, the GitHub token as the resource authorization_token (session.rs:211, sent at sessions.rs:172). The proxy operator and anyone on the path to the proxy can read all of this. So can whatever listens on the target port in the proxy's own loopback namespace. NO_PROXY handling is narrower than many users expect. Entries are split on ',' with no trimming (src/proxy.rs:579), so 'localhost, 127.0.0.1' yields the exact-host entry ' 127.0.0.1', which never matches. A present but empty NO_PROXY returns before no_proxy is read (src/proxy.rs:577-580). Calibration: the bash twin's curl also honours proxy variables, and the repository has no --noproxy or proxy override anywhere. The pattern is shared, which does not excuse the Rust finding. The source chain is complete, but no binary was built or run: the cleartext CONNECT tunnel is established from source and library source, not observed.
claimed_root_cause: The loopback-http exception in config::base_url_gate assumes the request reaches a socket on this host directly. transport::Http::new (rust/src/transport.rs:47) and transport::sessions::Http::new (rust/src/transport/sessions.rs:126) keep ureq 3.5.2's default Proxy::try_from_env(), so any ALL_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY variable (or its lowercase form) without a matching NO_PROXY entry diverts the plain-http request, key and tokens included, to a proxy host.

trace.description: Plain http://localhost[:port][/...], http://127.0.0.1... or http://[::1]... from --base-url, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or OPENAI_BASE_URL is accepted. Line 219 states the premise that the key never travels in clear over a network. The lower-trust input on this path is the process environment's implicit *_PROXY and NO_PROXY variables, which the architecture describes as 'often set for other tools'.
The gated provider and the API key go to transport::Http::new when ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY is unset. agent.rs:962 hands the same base URL and key to sessions::Http::new.

ureq::Agent::config_builder() starts from Config::default, whose proxy is Proxy::try_from_env() in ureq 3.5.2. Lines 47-52 add no .proxy(None), and neither does sessions.rs:126-131. Nothing in rust/src clears the proxy variables.
The API key goes into the x-api-key header (or Authorization: Bearer at line 81 for -p openai) of a POST to the plain-http loopback URL.

request.send(&body). If the environment names a proxy and NO_PROXY does not match, ureq's CONNECT connector opens 'CONNECT localhost:<port>' to the proxy host. The cleartext HTTP request, with the key header and any token-bearing body, then goes into that tunnel.

evidence.description: The stated invariant: plain http to a loopback host only, 'so the key never travels in clear over a network'.
The Messages transport's ureq config sets http_status_as_error(false), max_redirects(0), timeout_global and timeout_connect, and has no proxy override.

The sessions transport builds its calls, streams and downloads agents from config_builder() with no proxy override. The key goes in x-api-key at line 148 and in the upload header at line 224. Session-create bodies go out at line 172.

ureq = "=3.5.2". Cargo.lock:1256-1259 resolves 3.5.2 with checksum 3ac5cecf619ca81f66a96482db09687c9f7465af65f4300a8c30cca05bd5a59d, which equals the sha256 of ~/.cargo/registry/cache/.../ureq-3.5.2.crate. Read in that crate: Config::default proxy = Proxy::try_from_env() (src/config.rs:1073). try_from_env takes the first of ALL_PROXY/all_proxy/HTTPS_PROXY/https_proxy/HTTP_PROXY/http_proxy for every scheme (src/proxy.rs:232-249). connect_proxy_uri has no scheme check (src/config.rs:251-259). The CONNECT is skipped only when NO_PROXY matches (src/unversioned/transport/connect.rs:37-56, CONNECT line at 109). NO_PROXY is split on ',' without trimming (src/proxy.rs:579), and Http/Https proxies do not resolve the target locally (src/proxy.rs:56-59).
Messages bodies carry mcp_servers[].authorization_token from ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN[_<HOST>], which crosses the proxy in clear along with the key.
agent --repo session-create bodies carry the GitHub token as the github_repository resource's authorization_token. They are sent through sessions.rs:172 on the same proxied plain-http path.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox is available in this run, so the binary was not built or run against loopback fixtures with HTTP_PROXY set. The CONNECT tunnel carrying the cleartext key is established only from repository source plus checksum-verified ureq 3.5.2 source, not observed at runtime.

The decisive library behaviour (Config::default proxy from the environment, CONNECT tunnelling for http targets, untrimmed NO_PROXY entries) comes from the locally cached ureq-3.5.2 crate. Its sha256 equals the rust/Cargo.lock checksum, but it lies outside the repository and cannot be cited as a repository line.

Exposure depends on an environment fact outside source: whether users run a plain-http loopback --base-url, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or OPENAI_BASE_URL in a shell that exports ALL_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY (or a lowercase form) without a NO_PROXY entry matching that exact host form.

validation_plan.local: In an OS-enforced sandbox: external network disabled, read-only target, scratch-only writes, low CPU, memory and wall-clock limits. Build rust/ offline from the vendored lockfile. Start a loopback fixture on 127.0.0.1:3128 that logs every received byte to scratch and answers any CONNECT with 'HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established\r\n\r\n', then keeps reading. Leave nothing listening on 8080. Case 1: env -i HOME=$SCRATCH XDG_STATE_HOME=$SCRATCH ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=dummy-key-0000 HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3128 ask-claude --base-url http://localhost:8080 hi. Confirmed if the log shows 'CONNECT localhost:8080 HTTP/1.1' followed by a plaintext 'POST /v1/messages' carrying 'x-api-key: dummy-key-0000'. Case 2: as case 1 but with HTTPS_PROXY instead of HTTP_PROXY. Expect the same bytes, because the variable is scheme-agnostic. Case 3: add NO_PROXY=localhost. Expect no bytes at the fixture. Case 4: NO_PROXY='localhost, 127.0.0.1' with --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080. Expect bytes at the fixture, because of the untrimmed entry. Case 5: NO_PROXY='' together with no_proxy=localhost. Expect bytes. Case 6: --base-url http://[::1]:8080 with NO_PROXY=::1. Record whether the fixture receives bytes. Case 7: repeat case 1 for `ask-claude agent ...` with ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY unset and a dummy ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN, to cover sessions::Http and token-bearing bodies. Only dummy values are used throughout. After a fix, a unit test must pass: with HTTP_PROXY set, both Http::new constructors yield agents whose config().proxy() is None for an http:// root.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed and non-destructive: ask whether users who point ask-claude at a loopback http gateway or stub run it in shells, devcontainer images or corporate profiles that export ALL_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY (or a lowercase form). Ask whether those images set NO_PROXY or no_proxy to the exact host form used (localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]) without spaces after commas, and whether NO_PROXY is ever exported empty. Also ask whether the proxy in those environments is remote, or a local agent on this host (where the exposure narrows to that agent).
